props.title: The Ladies Man
props.initialSlug: Bumbling handyman causes chaos at all-women hotel

sections.content: Jerry Lewis's The Ladies Man stands as one of cinema's most innovative technical achievements, featuring a revolutionary multi-story dollhouse set that allowed simultaneous filming across multiple rooms. This architectural marvel predated Wes Anderson's similar approach in The Life Aquatic with Steve Zissou (2004) and The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014) by decades. Lewis's directing style here influenced countless filmmakers, particularly in his use of precisely choreographed physical comedy and fourth-wall breaks that would later inspire directors like Martin Scorsese, who paid homage in The King of Comedy (1982).

sections.content: The film's premise - a woman-fearing man working in a boarding house full of beautiful women - allows Lewis to explore gender dynamics through his signature combination of slapstick and social commentary. This approach influenced later comedy-of-discomfort works like Tootsie (1982) and Mrs. Doubtfire (1993), while maintaining a uniquely absurdist edge that would later inspire filmmakers like David Lynch, particularly in Wild at Heart (1990).

The technical innovation of the film cannot be overstated. The massive three-story set cost $350,000 in 1961 (equivalent to over $3 million today) and required revolutionary camera movements that influenced everything from Playtime (1967) to Russian Ark (2002). Lewis's attention to color coordination and production design created a template for later auteurs like Pedro Almodóvar and his vibrant visual style. SUBHEAD: Comedy Innovation and Technical Mastery

Lewis's directing techniques in The Ladies Man revolutionized comedy filmmaking through his use of the Video Assist system - technology he invented that allowed directors to immediately review takes. This innovation became industry standard and influenced directors from Francis Ford Coppola to Steven Spielberg. The film's elaborate staging and timing mechanics can be seen reflected in later works like Jacques Tati's Playtime (1967) and Blake Edwards' The Party (1968).
